title: Research Journal #38 — How We Verified BTLB-SIM on macOS and Windows
html:
Finishing What We Had Started

In Research Journal Entry 16, we described a problem familiar to almost every software developer: a program that works on one computer does not necessarily work the same way on another.

For Beyond the Light Barrier, this was more than a software inconvenience.

BTLB-SIM is being developed to support scientific calculations, preserve their inputs and results, and allow us to examine how those results were produced. If the software treats the same scientific record differently on macOS and Windows, we have a problem that could undermine confidence in our computational research.

Entry 16 documented the initial failures and the CP-002 correction while CP-003, the persistent-path issue, remained open. This retrospective records its closure and the acceptance of the combined corrections later on September 21.

On September 21, 2026, we reached the next milestone: we completed the defined macOS and Windows portability verification campaign for the corrected software.

The work was recorded under three related corrective efforts: CP-001B, CP-002, and CP-003.

The result was a PASS within the tested scope—but the story behind that result is as important as the PASS itself.

Three Problems That Looked Like One

At first, we were investigating whether BTLB-SIM could operate correctly across two different computer platforms.

The investigation exposed three distinct kinds of problems.

The first involved storing scientific records.

An earlier implementation assumed certain filesystem operations would work the same way across operating systems. In particular, the original artifact store relied on directory synchronization behavior that was appropriate to POSIX-style systems but not supported in the same way on Windows.

The corrected Store 2:0 successor introduced explicitly selected durability profiles. An early Windows checkout also exposed Git line-ending conversion in provenance-sensitive source files. The repository set a canonical LF checkout policy for those files.

The second involved the exact bytes of frozen scientific files.

A text file can look identical on two computers while having different underlying bytes. In CP-002, reading the frozen specification in text mode and re-encoding it changed the byte stream presented to the hash on Windows. The on-disk raw bytes matched the frozen reference.

That matters when the hash is supposed to verify that a scientific specification has not changed.

The project preserved the historical V1 implementation. Its V2 successor verifies the frozen specification’s raw bytes before decoding the text.

The third involved filesystem paths written into permanent scientific records.

macOS and Windows commonly represent file paths differently.

Consider a hypothetical file inside a research repository:

docs/experiments/example/specification.md

Windows might ordinarily represent the same relative location using backslashes:

docs\experiments\example\specification.md

If those platform-specific spellings become part of a permanent provenance record, two otherwise equivalent records can acquire different identities simply because they were created on different operating systems.

CP-003 introduced Execution 2:1, which uses canonical repository-relative paths with forward slashes for persistent provenance.

These three problems had different causes. Correcting one did not automatically correct the others.

Why We Preserved the Historical Implementations

One tempting way to finish a portability campaign is to repair every failing test until the entire test suite turns green.

We deliberately took a different approach.

BTLB-SIM preserves historical implementations and the records of their failures. That allows us to reconstruct what an earlier version actually did, including behavior that later versions corrected.

The corrected software therefore uses explicitly identified successor implementations rather than silently redefining the old ones.

This creates an unusual but important situation: the corrected software can pass its supported tests while older software in the same repository still fails on Windows.

Those are not contradictory results.

They answer different questions.

One asks whether the corrected implementation satisfies its current contract.

The other asks what happens when we also execute historical implementations that retain their original defects.

Both answers belong in the research record.

Building a Test That Could Not Quietly Ignore Problems

We needed a disciplined way to distinguish the two questions.

The result was the Cross-Platform Verification Profile v1.

The profile explicitly classifies test files as current, historical, or mixed. Scientific archive verification is handled separately.

A mixed test file requires additional care because it may contain both currently supported behavior and historical behavior that we intentionally preserve.

Just as importantly, the verification profile is designed to fail closed.

If a new top-level file matching tests/test_*.py appears without being classified, the profile rejects the inventory.

Duplicate or inconsistent classifications are also errors.

This matters because a passing test report is only meaningful when we know what was tested—and what was left out.

In one recorded development check, adding a new verification-profile test caused the profile itself to reject the previously unclassified test file. That was the intended behavior.

The verification gate was not supposed to become green by forgetting tests existed.

What Happened on macOS and Windows?

The project ran the current-software verification profile on both target development platforms at pre-merge candidate 6aebff55f650ada7e59be7852aa3e534ca81ad49.

On macOS 26.6.2, using ARM64 hardware and CPython 3.12.14, the gate reported:

688 tests passed, zero failed, zero skipped, and one explicitly historical mixed test deselected.

On native Windows 11 25H2, using AMD64 hardware and CPython 3.12.10, the same current-software gate reported:

679 tests passed, zero failed, nine skipped, and one explicitly historical mixed test deselected.

The counts reconcile: 679 Windows passes plus nine Windows skips account for the same 688 selected current tests.

But those nine skips are not passes.

The correct conclusion is that the selected current software gate completed without test failures in both recorded environments, subject to its explicit exclusions and skips.

It would be incorrect to claim that all 688 tests passed on Windows.

What About the 109 Windows Failures?

The broader Windows test run provides an equally important part of the record.

When the project executed the entire repository suite, including preserved historical implementations, it reported:

851 collected, with 733 passed, 109 failed, and nine skipped.

Those failures were not discarded.

The project’s CP-003 verification record associates the failures with preserved historical portability problems in artifact storage, frozen-file hashing, and persistent-path spelling. This run preceded the committed current verification profile.

The complete repository did not pass on Windows.

That remains true even though the corrected current-software verification gate passed.

For Beyond the Light Barrier, this is not a reason to hide the broader result. It is a reason to state exactly which software was verified and why other software still fails.

A historical failure can remain useful evidence long after a corrected successor has been accepted.

Checking the Software After the Merge

The portability corrections were then brought together on the project's main development line.

A successful test before merging is useful, but it does not automatically establish that the merged version still behaves as expected.

The project ran the current-software verification gate again on merge commit 4543b1fa12b05865c226557f0cf70fffdf6fa97a, using macOS 26.6.2 on ARM64, CPython 3.12.14, and pytest 9.1.1.

688 passed, zero failed, with one explicitly historical mixed test deselected.

The project also rechecked two previously frozen scientific archives:

  • VAPE-1-R1: archive verification passed for 10 cases and 98 content-addressed objects.
  • WC-PO-1.7C-V1: archive verification passed for 725 immutable objects.

The archive checks confirmed the recorded integrity properties of both frozen archives on the merge commit.

The native Windows current-gate result belonged to the pre-merge correction candidate. The merged-main acceptance record retained that result; it did not claim a separate native Windows rerun on the merged commit.

That distinction is part of the evidence.

On September 21, 2026, the combined CP-001B through CP-003 portability correction campaign received its recorded CLOSED — PASS disposition.

What We Had—and Had Not—Verified

The completed campaign established a bounded software-engineering result.

Within the recorded macOS and Windows environments, the corrected software satisfied the defined current-software verification gates.

It also demonstrated that important differences between operating systems—filesystem operations, file-byte handling, and path representation—could be addressed without erasing the historical software or its failures.

But the campaign did not verify every possible operating environment.

It did not establish native Linux portability, support for arbitrary filesystems, or physical power-loss durability.

The Windows file-sync profile covers file flushing and synchronization. Directory-entry crash durability is outside that profile.

Nor did cross-platform testing independently reproduce the underlying scientific theories or experiments.

The frozen WC-PO-1.7C-V1 numerical results remained Category 7, with Category 6 analytic benchmarks. Running or checking their software and archives on the supported development platforms did not promote them to Category 8 independent reproduction or Category 9 physical experimental evidence.

No new gravitational effect, wormhole, warp drive, or faster-than-light capability was demonstrated by this portability work.

Why This Milestone Matters

The obvious result is that we could now use a corrected BTLB-SIM software path under a defined verification profile on macOS and Windows.

The more important result is that we established clearer boundaries around what a passing software test actually means.

A pass should identify the software version, the environment, the tests selected, the tests skipped, and the historical behaviors excluded from that particular gate.

A failure should remain available for examination, even after a successor corrects it.

And a verified software implementation should never be confused with independent scientific confirmation of the physics being investigated.

The portability campaign gave us a more dependable foundation for the next stage of work.

The merged-main acceptance record was committed at 2:34 p.m. Central Daylight Time on September 21. About twenty minutes later, at 2:54 p.m., the project committed the scope freeze for AR-1.7, its Architecture Stress Audit. Entry 17 introduced the stress audit on September 22.

That next investigation would ask a different question.

We had tested whether the corrected framework behaved appropriately across two development platforms.

Now we wanted to investigate how the architecture behaved under deliberately difficult conditions—and where its design might still fail.

The portability milestone did not mean that BTLB-SIM was finished.

It meant that one carefully defined set of problems had been resolved, its evidence preserved, and the next questions could be investigated from a better-understood baseline.

Research Status

Historical milestone: September 21, 2026.

Disposition: CP-001B through CP-003 — CLOSED, PASS within the defined macOS and Windows portability verification scope.

Evidence classification: Internal software verification and research-infrastructure development. No promotion of underlying scientific evidence categories. No independent scientific reproduction or physical experimental result.

Remaining limitations: Historical Windows failures remain preserved; nine current-gate Windows tests were skipped; native Linux, arbitrary-filesystem behavior, and physical power-loss durability were not established.

Sources and Research Records

  1. Beyond the Light Barrier, Research Journal Entry 16 — When “Works on My Computer” Isn’t Good Enough, September 21, 2026. Read Journal Entry 16
  2. Beyond the Light Barrier, Research Journal Entry 17 — What Happens When We Try to Break It?, September 22, 2026. Read Journal Entry 17
  3. BTLB-SIM, CP-001B portable storage. Open or download README.md from the folder and search for the heading “CP-001B portable storage”.
  4. BTLB-SIM, CP-002 frozen byte identity. Open or download README.md from the folder and search for the heading “CP-002 frozen byte identity”.
  5. BTLB-SIM, CP-003 persistent provenance paths. Open or download README.md from the folder and search for the heading “CP-003 persistent provenance paths”.
  6. BTLB-SIM, Current gate and merged acceptance. Open or download README.md from the folder and search for the heading “Current gate and merged acceptance”.

The supporting supplement provides selected extracts from the project's pinned records, plus the source identifiers and checksums. The complete source records require repository access.

The supplement reports historical test outcomes from contemporaneous project records. Full test output for the exact closure gates and the historical-inclusive Windows run was unavailable for review. The published extracts support review of the reported counts and scope. A test-by-test audit would require the original full output.
